claim: Models that can solve a problem often cannot falsify a near-correct solution to it: the best reasoning model makes a valid counterexample for under about 9 percent of REFUTE cases while its rating implies about 49 percent solve rate. TestCase-Eval (43.8 percent vs 93.3 percent human) points the same way.
agent_test: On our tasks, measure solve rate vs rate of producing a failing input for a planted subtle bug at equal tokens.
audit_note: Minor: REFUTE abstract says up to 48% while Table gives 48.7% for o3-mini (high), so 'about 49' is fine; the TestCase-Eval comparison is a different task so 'points the same way' is loose.

claim: Giving the model the correct solution or code-execution feedback does not close the falsification gap (REFUTE cells stay in the 1 to 10 percent band).
agent_test: Add the oracle answer to the S7 prompt arm and check whether test success moves.

claim: Prompting an explicit randomized search plus brute-force checker gives only marginal gains for chat models and lowers success for most reasoning models (REFUTE: DeepSeek-V3 4.0, R1 4.0, Flash Thinking 3.7, o3-mini 8.3 percent, where o3-mini doubled its rate and solved cases other strategies missed); about 35 percent of runs end in an invalid counterexample, 86 percent of those from wrong brute-force code. SymCE adds that a model fine-tuned only on counterexamples fabricates a witness for true theorems (true-theorem Pass@1 0.27 to 0.00) because it learns the counterexample output form without the negated-conclusion constraint.
agent_test: Compare free-form vs generator-plus-checker S7 at equal tokens; count invalid counterexamples.
audit_note: REFUTE says randomized-search prompting gives only marginal gains for chat models and that reasoning models' performance deteriorates (o3-mini is the exception, doubling to 8.3 with mostly disjoint successes), not that it 'helps weaker chat models' while reasoning models 'gain little'; 35% invalid runs (86% wrong brute force) and SymCE 0.27 to 0.00 match.
claim_before_audit: Prompting an explicit randomized search plus brute-force checker helps weaker chat models; reasoning models gain little in absolute terms; about 35 percent of runs yield an invalid counterexample. SymCE adds that a model trained to always emit a witness fabricates one for true theorems (true-theorem recognition 0.27 to 0.00) mostly by not negating the conclusion.

claim: Counterexample success is not predicted by problem difficulty, author skill or tests passed; different strategies solve different cases, so a portfolio of strategies adds coverage.
agent_test: Run two S7 strategies and measure union vs best single at equal total tokens.

claim: Chain-of-thought beats direct output for writing fault-exposing tests; reasoning models lead; Python solutions are easier to break than C++ or Java.
agent_test: Add a think-before-test step and compare to direct test output at equal tokens.

claim: There is a trade-off between tests that expose a fault and tests whose expected output the model predicts correctly; tests that break code are harder cases.
agent_test: Score expected-output accuracy separately for adversarial and ordinary tests; prefer executing code over predicting its output.

claim: Generated tests that attack code also work as a selector for best-of-N and beat an 8B trained reward model on some settings.
agent_test: Use S7 tests as the selector among candidate answers vs majority vote at equal tokens.

claim: On CounterMath, saying a statement is false is much easier than giving a valid counterexample: strict rationale scores sit well below judgement F1 for every model (e.g. Gemini 2.5 Pro 77.0 F1 vs 65.1 strict).
agent_test: Score our agent separately on the verdict and on the quality of the exhibited counterexample.

claim: Reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 80.7, Gemini 2.5 Pro 77.0 F1) lead CounterMath; most open math models sit near 30 F1.
agent_test: Not an agent test; baseline expectation.

claim: Fine-tuning on about 1,000 counterexample samples gives small in-domain gains (F1 38.3 to 41.1) and larger but noisy out-of-distribution gains (MATH 80.5 to 87.9; AIME 20 to 30, a 30-problem set). INSPIRE, a second method, finds out-of-distribution gains near zero: AIME 2024 unchanged for two of three models, +6.67 (2 problems) for the third; MATH500 +0.6 to +1.8. Both papers are single runs without confidence intervals, so the CounterMath out-of-distribution gain is probably noise-level.
agent_test: Needs training; we do not train. Note only.

claim: LLMs repeat Wason's 2-4-6 error: they mostly propose tests that fit their own guess. Success ranges 6 to 78 percent over 11 models and rises with the share of incompatible tests. WILT independently finds the best model solves only 14 of 50 hidden rules.
agent_test: Log the share of S7 tests that could contradict the current hypothesis; correlate with success.
audit_note: Minor: WILT best is 14/50 = 28% (Jhaveri et al. cite it as 26%); the two papers are independent.

claim: A Think-in-Opposites prompt (build a test opposite to the last one) lifts rule discovery from 42 to 56 percent on average; a dual-goal prompt gives similar gains.
agent_test: Insert the opposite-test instruction in S7 and compare at equal tokens.

claim: Thinking mode raises Wason-task success but not reliably the incompatible-test share, so extra reasoning helps for reasons other than falsification.
agent_test: Compare a thinking-budget arm with a TiO-prompt arm at equal tokens.

claim: Test proposal and rule deduction are separate skills: o1-mini with another model's tests guessed 19 of 50 rules vs 13 alone.
agent_test: Try splitting test design from hypothesis update into separate calls.

claim: Positive testing is not itself an error (Klayman and Ha: it reveals a wrong rule when the true rule is narrower than the guess and fails in the other cases). Rival accounts (Evans: failure to think of falsifiers) disagree on cause.
agent_test: Mix positive and negative tests and see which finds the error first on our tasks.

claim: Mace4 and Paradox-style finite model finders search finite structures of growing size for a model of the denied conjecture and return a countermodel; Mace4 starts at domain size 2 and replaced Mace2's SAT flattening, which blew up. On satisfiable TPTP problems at 300 s Paradox solves about 87 percent (1083 of 1251, TPTP 3.1.1) and Mace4 about 64 percent (802 of 1251); on TPTP 5.4.0 Paradox 1450, CVC4 finite model finder 1277, Z3 941.
agent_test: Offer the agent a finite-model-search tool on small logic problems and measure refutation rate.

claim: Nitpick searches scopes (default 1 to 10 per type, 30 s timeout), prunes with scope monotonicity, and can return spurious counterexamples for coinductive types. In its own evaluation (3200 mutants, 10 s) it found genuine counterexamples on most of 20 Isabelle theories, usually within seconds, beat Refute 293 to 214 on the TPTP higher-order model-finding run, and exposed 3 bugs in provers; it is weak on real arithmetic and large state spaces.
agent_test: Always re-check a found counterexample against the original claim before accepting it.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-01 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: A model finder inside an SMT solver (CVC4) solved 723 of 793 random colouring problems with the best variant vs 617 for a MACE-style encoding (60 s limit). On satisfiable TPTP at 300 s, Paradox (1450) still beat CVC4 (1277) and Z3 (941), but CVC4 solved 52 that Paradox did not.
agent_test: Not an agent test.

claim: Deep cross-entropy RL with no prior knowledge found explicit counterexamples to open graph conjectures (n=19 tree, value 5.16 vs bound 5.24; a 203-vertex graph).
agent_test: Use search-with-verifier loops on constructive conjectures; compare to single-shot at equal tokens.

claim: PatternBoost (local search plus transformer) found a 6-cube spanning subgraph with 81 edges and diameter 6, below the 82 edges conjectured minimal by Graham, refuting a conjecture open for about 30 years. Earlier work by one of its authors (Wagner 2021, cross-entropy reinforcement learning) refuted several younger open conjectures in graph theory, so learned search can disprove published conjectures.
agent_test: Same as above.
audit_note: PatternBoost numbers check out (81 edges vs conjectured 82, a 30-year-old Graham conjecture), but Wagner (2021) is a co-author of PatternBoost (not independent) and his refuted conjectures (e.g. Aouchiche-Hansen, about 2010) were not decades old, so 'conjectures that stood for decades' over-reads the pair.
claim_before_audit: PatternBoost (local search plus transformer) found a 6-cube subgraph with 81 edges and diameter 6, below the conjectured minimum of 82. Together with Wagner (2021) this shows learned search can refute conjectures that stood for decades.

claim: LLM-guided evolutionary search (AlphaEvolve) found no counterexample on several conjectures and repeatedly exploited weak verifiers (float leaks). A second search paper reports weaker open-source results.
agent_test: Use an exact checker (rational arithmetic) for every counterexample the agent claims.
audit_note: Minor: 'weaker open-source results' is vague; the second paper (Ellenberg et al.) shows its open-source FunSearch reimplementation falling short of the known cap-set score 512 (best 448) and of PatternBoost on no-isosceles (96 vs 110), not a head-to-head with AlphaEvolve.

claim: On 200 random arXiv conjectures, GPT models gave 70 counterexamples and 55 proofs. About 60 percent of the verified early counterexamples were off-the-shelf textbook examples, and trivial cases such as the trivial group or a single vertex appear. All review was by the same model family; no expert review exists, so the non-trivial survival rate is unknown.
agent_test: Check any counterexample against the claim's intended hypotheses before treating it as a refutation.

claim: Training a model to give a counterexample and prove it in Lean 4 raises pass@1 on FOR-COUNTER (1,058 formalized CounterMath problems) from 127 solved (strongest baseline) to 222; pass@9 224 to 302. Confirmed from the primary paper (marked rejected from ICLR 2026; the authors report counts because the autoformalized benchmark has errors).
agent_test: Needs training; with Lean as external checker the verification part is testable.

claim: Models find that a reasoning trace is wrong far less well than they fix it once told where: best step-level mistake finding 52.87 percent (GPT-4); oracle-location backtracking gives +18 to +44 points on corrected cases.
agent_test: Add a locate-the-first-error step and compare to whole-trace review at equal tokens.

claim: Intrinsic self-review without outside feedback does not help and can hurt (GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 41.8); with an oracle label it helps (GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3).
agent_test: Tie S7 to an external check (execution, checker), not self-judgement.

claim: LLM critics (CriticGPT) catch more bugs than paid contractors but hallucinate bugs; critiques were preferred in 63 percent of naturally occurring bug cases. Executed-counterexample training (ARBITER) raises hack success on wrong programs from 40.61 to 62.67 percent, and counterexamples track diagnosis quality: among compilable candidates a counterexample succeeds for 71.6 percent of correct diagnoses versus 10.3 percent of incorrect or vacuous ones.
agent_test: Add a critic role in S7 and count false alarms.
audit_note: CriticGPT (63%, more bugs than contractors, hallucinations) and ARBITER 40.61 to 62.67 match, but the audit reports P(counterexample succeeds | diagnosis correct)=71.6% vs 10.3% for incorrect diagnoses, not that the failing input predicts a right diagnosis; the direction is reversed.
claim_before_audit: LLM critics (CriticGPT) find more inserted bugs than paid contractors but hallucinate; critiques were preferred in 63 percent of natural bug cases. Executed-counterexample training (ARBITER) raises hack success on wrong programs 40.61 to 62.67 percent, and the failing input predicts a right diagnosis 71.6 versus 10.3 percent.

claim: Code models mistake plausible wrong programs for correct ones (about 60 percent accuracy against 50 percent chance).
agent_test: Execute rather than inspect.

claim: Counterexamples drive discovery in mathematics (Lakatos): a refutation can lead to repairing the claim rather than dropping it. Not opened this run.
agent_test: Test whether a claim-repair step after refutation beats plain retry.

claim: Giving an LLM a finite-model finder (Mace4, Nitpick, SMT model) raises refutation rate over unaided reasoning at equal tokens: NO DIRECT STUDY FOUND. Nearest evidence: a symbolic solver raises accuracy a lot when the claim translates cleanly (GPT-4 ProofWriter 68.11 CoT to 79.66, LogicalDeduction 75.25 to 87.63) and loses when it does not (PrOntoQA 98.79 CoT vs 83.20); LLM search beats numeric optimizers on 14 of 21 cyber-physical specs but fails completely on others.
agent_test: Run the small-claim set with and without a Nitpick or Mace4 call at equal tokens; count valid refutations.

claim: An exact external checker removes most invalid counterexamples but not all: a per-theorem verifier was 97.7 percent accurate on 177 audited decisions; legal-input-plus-checker verification is how ARBITER defines success. A model trained to always find a counterexample produces invalid ones (true-theorem recognition fell from 0.27 to 0.00 under SFT).
agent_test: Code check of every hypothesis and the negated conclusion before accepting a refutation; allow 'none found'.
audit_note: Minor: 97.7% is 173/177 decision accuracy of the verifier (accept and reject decisions), which supports 'not perfect' rather than a rate of remaining invalid counterexamples.

claim: Counterexample training does not give reliable general reasoning gains: INSPIRE shows AIME 2024 unchanged for 2 of 3 models and +2 problems for the third, MATH500 +0.6 to +1.8, GSM8K +0.5 to +1.1; no confidence intervals in either that or CounterMath.
agent_test: Note only; we do not train.

claim: Mace4 is weaker than Paradox on satisfiable TPTP problems (802 vs 1083 of 1251, 300 s, TPTP 3.1.1); a third finder (FM-Darwin, 1074) solves 328 problems Mace4 cannot. Solved sets overlap only partly, so a portfolio of finders adds coverage.
agent_test: If a model finder is offered, prefer a Paradox-class tool or a portfolio, and set a 300 s class limit only for offline use.
audit_note: Minor: the Mace4/Paradox/FM-Darwin figures (802, 1083, 1074 of 1251, 328 problems Mace4 cannot solve, partial overlap) are from Baumgartner et al. alone; Reynolds et al. is on TPTP 5.4.0 and does not include Mace4, so the portfolio inference rests on one comparison.

claim: In test generation for code, a cheap random property-based generator matched an adaptive LLM tester at equal test counts (difference -0.024, 95 percent CI [-0.097,+0.043]), while both beat a fixed LLM-written test set by about 0.11 to 0.13 failure-rate points; showing the tester the candidate source added nothing (-0.005, CI [-0.044,+0.034]).
agent_test: Include a random or property arm in every S7 portfolio; measure the LLM arm's marginal gain over it.

claim: LLM-driven falsification search and numeric optimizers have complementary wins: the LLM ranked first on 14 of 21 cyber-physical specs (one simulation on 6) but found nothing on some specs where an optimizer succeeded 10 of 10. This supports a union of strategies; the equal-token union gain is still unmeasured.
agent_test: Run LLM-semantic and blind-numeric arms on the same spec set and measure union gain.

claim: Adversarially generated tests are a useful selector but not a substitute for trusted tests: self-generated test selection lifted a 7B model from 28.56 to 43.01 pass@1 vs 45.99 for curated public tests and 46.15 for both.
agent_test: Use generated tests to rank candidates but keep trusted tests when they exist.

claim: Whether a check-intended-hypotheses step raises the share of non-trivial counterexamples is untested. Nearest data: reviewer instances of the same model flagged a significant portion of early counterexamples as resting on imprecise statements; there is no expert review.
agent_test: Add an 'inside the intended domain' check and measure the drop in trivial counterexamples against an expert or independent-model audit.
